props.title: One Night at McCool's

sections.content: One Night at McCool's (2001) stands as a quirky dark comedy that plays with multiple perspectives in the vein of Rashomon (1950), but with a decidedly neo-noir twist. Starring Liv Tyler as the femme fatale Jewel, the film follows three different men's accounts of the same deadly night, each viewing her through their own warped lens. The film's structure mirrors similar perspective-shifting narratives like Go (1999) and Jackie Brown (1997), where reality bends based on who's telling the story.

movies.title: The Last Seduction
movies.slug: A femme fatale fleeing with stolen money manipulates a small-town man into her deadly schemes

sections.content: Director Harald Zwart crafts a neo-noir that deliberately plays with genre conventions, much like The Last Seduction (1994) or Body Heat (1981). Matt Dillon, Paul Reiser, and John Goodman each bring distinct energy to their lovestruck characters, while Michael Douglas delivers a scene-stealing performance as a hitman with a ridiculous pompadour. The film's dark humor and violence echo the Coen Brothers' style in Fargo (1996), blending comedy with genuine menace.

What sets One Night at McCool's apart is how it subverts femme fatale tropes while still embracing them. Unlike classic noirs like Double Indemnity (1944), Jewel isn't just manipulating men for money - she's obsessed with creating her perfect domestic life, albeit through horrifically twisted means. This puts the film in conversation with other darkly comic examinations of the American Dream like American Beauty (1999) and To Die For (1995). SUBHEAD: Dark Comedy Meets Neo-Noir

movies.title: Wild Things
movies.slug: A complex tale of betrayal and seduction unfolds through multiple perspectives in South Florida

sections.content: The film's strongest moments come from its ability to shift tone rapidly while maintaining coherence. Each man's perspective of Jewel reveals more about their own delusions than about her true nature. This narrative technique recalls The Usual Suspects (1995), where unreliable narration drives both plot and character development. The film's violence, while extreme, serves the comedy in ways similar to Very Bad Things (1998) or Grosse Pointe Blank (1997).
